notes.front: What is Azure SQL Database?
notes.back: A fully managed SQL Server database engine in Azure, based on the latest stable Enterprise Edition of SQL Server.
notes.explanation: Microsoft owns, hosts and maintains the standardised hardware and software it runs on.
notes.example: Like running SQL Server yourself, but without owning a server: you create a database and Azure runs the engine.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Azure SQL Database”
notes.evidence: A fully managed SQL Server database engine, based on the latest stable Enterprise Edition of SQL Server. SQL Database is built on standardized hardware and software that is owned, hosted, and maintained by Microsoft.

notes.front: What is Azure SQL Managed Instance?
notes.back: A platform-as-a-service database engine with near 100% compatibility with the latest Enterprise Edition SQL Server engine.
notes.explanation: It also gives a native virtual network implementation, which addresses common security concerns.
notes.example: Like a whole SQL Server instance you used to run in your own data centre, but hosted and looked after by Azure.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL Managed Instance? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Overview”
notes.evidence: Azure SQL Managed Instance is a PaaS service that has near 100% compatibility with the latest Enterprise Edition SQL Server Database Engine. It provides a native [virtual network (VNet)](/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-overview) implementation that addresses common security concerns,

notes.front: What is SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines?
notes.back: SQL Server installed and hosted on Windows Server or Linux virtual machines in Azure: the infrastructure-as-a-service option.
notes.explanation: Every supported version and edition of SQL Server can be installed on such a machine.
notes.example: Like renting a server in Azure and installing SQL Server on it yourself, much as you would in your own data centre.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “SQL Server on Azure VMs”
notes.evidence: SQL Server installed and hosted in the cloud runs on Windows Server or Linux virtual machines in Azure. All supported versions and editions of SQL Server are available to install in an IaaS virtual machine.
introduces: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
uses: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

notes.front: What is a database transaction unit (DTU)?
notes.back: A blended measure of processor, memory, reads and writes, used to size Azure SQL databases.
notes.explanation: The DTU model sells these units in compute sizes, each with fixed included storage, fixed backup retention and a fixed price.
notes.example: Like buying a car by one overall power rating instead of choosing the engine, gearbox and tyres separately.
notes.source: DTU-based purchasing model overview (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Database transaction units (DTUs)”
notes.evidence: A database transaction unit (DTU) represents a blended measure of CPU, memory, reads, and writes. Service tiers in the DTU-based purchasing model are differentiated by a range of compute sizes with a fixed amount of included storage, fixed retention period for backups, and fixed price.

notes.front: What is an elastic pool in Azure SQL Database?
notes.back: A collection of single databases that share one set of resources, such as processor and memory.
notes.explanation: Databases can be moved into and out of a pool, so the grouping is not fixed for ever.
notes.example: Like a team sharing one printer budget instead of each person buying a printer they rarely use.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL Database? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Deployment models”
notes.evidence: [Elastic pool](elastic-pool-overview.md) is a collection of single databases with a shared set of resources, such as CPU or memory. Single databases can be moved into and out of an elastic pool.

notes.front: What is an elastic database transaction unit (eDTU)?
notes.back: The unit of shared capacity in an elastic pool under the DTU model: the pool gets a set number for a set price.
notes.explanation: Each database in the pool draws more of them under heavy load and fewer under light load, within configured limits.
notes.example: Like a household data allowance shared by several phones, rather than a separate allowance for each phone.
notes.source: DTU-based purchasing model overview (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Elastic database transaction units (eDTUs)”
notes.evidence: A pool is given a set number of eDTUs for a set price. In the elastic pool, individual databases can autoscale within the configured boundaries. A database under a heavier load consumes more eDTUs to meet demand.

notes.front: What is the General Purpose service tier of Azure SQL Database?
notes.back: The default service tier in the vCore model, designed for most generic workloads.
notes.explanation: It fits most workloads; you move to Business Critical for low-latency local storage, or to Hyperscale for very large databases.
notes.example: Like standard class on a train: where most passengers travel unless they need something special.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “When to choose the General Purpose service tier”
notes.evidence: The General Purpose service tier is the default service tier in Azure SQL Database designed for most of generic workloads.

notes.front: What is the Business Critical service tier?
notes.back: A vCore service tier where each database runs on a four-node cluster, with compute and storage together on every node.
notes.explanation: Data is replicated between the nodes for high availability, and each node keeps it on locally attached solid-state storage.
notes.example: Like keeping four synchronised copies of a ledger at four clerks’ desks instead of one copy in a distant archive.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Business Critical”
notes.evidence: In the Business Critical model, compute and storage is integrated on each node. Replication of data between database engine processes on each node of a four-node cluster achieves high availability, with each node using locally attached SSD as data storage.

notes.front: What is the Hyperscale service tier?
notes.back: A vCore service tier of Azure SQL Database with independently scalable compute and storage, suitable for all workload types.
notes.explanation: Its compute and storage resources substantially exceed those of General Purpose and Business Critical.
notes.example: Like a warehouse whose floor space and loading staff can each be expanded separately, without moving building.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Hyperscale”
notes.evidence: The Hyperscale service tier is suitable for all workload types. Its cloud native architecture provides independently scalable compute and storage to support the widest variety of traditional and modern applications. Compute and storage resources in Hyperscale substantially exceed the resources available in the General Purpose and Business Critical tiers.

notes.front: What is sharding?
notes.back: Distributing large amounts of identically structured data across many independent databases.
notes.explanation: It is especially popular with developers building software-as-a-service products whose customers are called tenants.
notes.example: Like splitting a phone book into volumes A–F, G–M and so on, each volume laid out the same way.
notes.source: Scale out with Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Sharding”
notes.evidence: *Sharding* is a technique to distribute large amounts of identically structured data across many independent databases. It is especially popular with cloud developers creating Software as a Service (SAAS) offerings for end customers or businesses. These end customers are often referred to as "tenants."

notes.front: What does read scale-out do in Azure SQL?
notes.back: It runs read-only workloads on the compute of a read-only replica instead of on the read-write replica.
notes.explanation: Isolating those reads keeps them from affecting the performance of the read-write workload.
notes.example: Like sending visitors who only want to browse to a reading room of copies, so the clerks updating the originals are not disturbed.
notes.source: Use read-only replicas to offload read-only query workloads (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Use read-only replicas to offload read-only query workloads”
notes.evidence: The *read scale-out* feature allows you to offload read-only workloads using the compute capacity of one of the read-only replicas, instead of running them on the read-write replica. This way, some read-only workloads can be isolated from the read-write workloads, and don't affect their performance.

notes.front: What is transparent data encryption (TDE)?
notes.back: Real-time encryption and decryption of the database, its backups and its transaction log files at rest, with no application changes.
notes.explanation: Its purpose is protection against the threat of malicious offline activity.
notes.example: Like a filing cabinet that locks every drawer as papers go in and unlocks as an authorised clerk takes them out, without the clerk working any differently.
notes.source: Transparent data encryption for SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Transparent data encryption for SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics”
notes.evidence: helps protect Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics against the threat of malicious offline activity by encrypting data at rest. It performs real-time encryption and decryption of the database, associated backups, and transaction log files at rest without requiring changes to the application.

notes.front: What is dynamic data masking?
notes.back: A policy-based feature that hides sensitive data in query results, while the data stored in the database is unchanged.
notes.explanation: You decide how much of the sensitive data to reveal, with minimal effect on the application layer.
notes.example: Like a receptionist’s screen that shows a visitor’s name but blanks out their home address, while the full record stays on file.
notes.source: Dynamic data masking (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Dynamic data masking”
notes.evidence: Dynamic data masking helps prevent unauthorized access to sensitive data by enabling customers to designate how much of the sensitive data to reveal with minimal effect on the application layer. It's a policy-based security feature that hides the sensitive data in the result set of a query over designated database fields, while the data in the database isn't changed.

notes.front: What is Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server?
notes.back: Microsoft’s fully managed service for running community versions of PostgreSQL, with fine-grained control over configuration.
notes.explanation: You keep detailed control of server settings, and can choose high availability within one availability zone or across several.
notes.example: Like Azure SQL Database, but for applications built on the open-source PostgreSQL engine instead of SQL Server.
notes.source: What is Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server? (Microsoft Learn), “What is Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
introduces: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server
uses: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server

notes.front: Which database engine do all the Azure SQL products use?
notes.back: The SQL Server database engine.
notes.explanation: Because it is the familiar engine, applications can be migrated with ease.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “What is Azure SQL?”
notes.evidence: Azure SQL is a family of managed, secure, and intelligent products that use the SQL Server database engine in the Azure cloud. Azure SQL is built upon the familiar SQL Server engine, so you can migrate applications with ease

notes.front: Choosing between the platform and infrastructure options for SQL Server in Azure, what is the key question to ask?
notes.back: Do you want to manage the database, apply patches and take backups yourself, or delegate those operations to Azure?
notes.explanation: Delegating these tasks points to a platform-as-a-service option; keeping them points to infrastructure as a service.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Service comparison”
notes.evidence: The key question that you need to ask when deciding between PaaS or IaaS is - do you want to manage your database, apply patches, and take backups - or do you want to delegate these operations to Azure?

notes.front: Which member of the Azure SQL family is infrastructure as a service?
notes.back: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines.
notes.explanation: What Azure provides is the virtual machine; SQL Server runs inside it.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “SQL Server on Azure VMs”
notes.evidence: [SQL Server on Azure VMs](virtual-machines/windows/sql-server-on-azure-vm-iaas-what-is-overview.md) falls into the industry category *Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS)* and allows you to run SQL Server inside a fully managed virtual machine (VM) in Azure.
uses: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

notes.front: Which member of the Azure SQL family does Microsoft call best for most migrations to the cloud?
notes.back: Azure SQL Managed Instance.
notes.explanation: It is a lift-and-shift-ready collection of system and user databases sharing one set of resources, like a SQL Server instance.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Azure SQL Managed Instance”
notes.evidence: falls into the industry category of *Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS)*, and is best for most migrations to the cloud. SQL Managed Instance is a collection of system and user databases with a shared set of resources that is lift-and-shift ready.
uses: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

notes.front: Which member of the Azure SQL family is described as best for modern cloud applications that want the latest stable SQL Server features under tight development and marketing deadlines?
notes.back: Azure SQL Database.
notes.explanation: Of the three, it is the relational database-as-a-service, aimed at modern cloud applications.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Azure SQL Database”
notes.evidence: Best for modern cloud applications that want to use the latest stable SQL Server features and have time constraints in development and marketing.
uses: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

notes.front: What does Azure SQL Managed Instance add to the platform benefits of Azure SQL Database?
notes.back: Extra capabilities such as a native virtual network, and full SQL Server access and feature compatibility for migrating instances.
notes.explanation: This is what lets databases move from on-premises with minimal to no database changes.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Azure SQL Managed Instance”
notes.evidence: SQL Managed Instance supports database migration from on-premises with minimal to no database changes. This option provides all of the PaaS benefits of Azure SQL Database but adds additional capabilities, such as native virtual network. SQL Managed Instance provides full SQL Server access and feature compatibility to migrate your SQL Server instances to Azure.

notes.front: A company wants to move 40 on-premises SQL Server instances to Azure with as few database changes as possible, and does not want to patch software or run backups itself. Which option fits best?
notes.back: Azure SQL Managed Instance.
notes.choices:
A) Azure SQL Managed Instance
B) SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
C) Azure SQL Database single databases
notes.choicesExplained: B: it keeps compatibility, but patching, backups and the operating system stay with the company. C: single databases are also fully managed, but Managed Instance has near 100% SQL Server compatibility, so it needs the fewest database changes.
notes.explanation: Managed Instance takes existing applications across with minimal changes and still provides automatic patching, backups and high availability.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL Managed Instance? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Overview”
notes.evidence: SQL Managed Instance enables existing SQL Server customers to lift and shift their on-premises applications to the cloud with minimal application and database changes. At the same time, SQL Managed Instance provides all PaaS capabilities (automatic patching and version updates, [automated backups](automated-backups-overview.md), [high availability](high-availability-sla-local-zone-redundancy.md)) to drastically reduce management overhead
uses: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

notes.front: What is the most significant difference between SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines and the two platform options?
notes.back: It gives full control over the database engine.
notes.explanation: You choose when maintenance such as system updates happens, and can even change the recovery model to simple or bulk-logged.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “SQL Server on Azure VMs”
notes.evidence: The most significant difference from SQL Database and SQL Managed Instance is that SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines allows full control over the database engine. You can choose when to start maintenance activities including system updates, change the recovery model to simple or bulk-logged,
uses: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

notes.front: A vendor’s application needs its own monitoring agent installed on the database server’s operating system. Which Azure SQL option allows that?
notes.back: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines.
notes.choices:
A) SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
B) Azure SQL Managed Instance
C) Azure SQL Database
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: with the platform options you no longer manage the operating system, so there is no server on which to install software.
notes.explanation: Only the virtual machine option gives full control of the operating system, including installing extra software.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Administration”
notes.evidence: With **SQL Server on Azure VMs**, you have full control over the operating system and SQL Server instance configuration. With a VM, it's up to you to decide when to update/upgrade the operating system and database software and when to install any extra software such as anti-virus.
uses: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

notes.front: With Azure SQL Database or Azure SQL Managed Instance, what are two things you still administer yourself?
notes.back: Any two of: databases and logins; index and query tuning; auditing and security.
notes.explanation: What you stop managing is the database engine, the operating system and the hardware.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Administration”
notes.evidence: With **SQL Database** and **SQL Managed Instance**, you can continue to administer your database, but you no longer need to manage the database engine, operating system, or the hardware. Examples of items you can continue to administer include databases and logins, index and query tuning, and auditing and security.

notes.front: Which Azure SQL Database deployment option gives each database its own guaranteed compute, memory and storage?
notes.back: A single database.
notes.explanation: Those resources are dedicated to it and not shared with other databases, unlike a pool.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL Database? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Scalable performance and pools”
notes.evidence: With single databases, each database is isolated from others and is portable. Each database has its own guaranteed amount of compute, memory, and storage resources. The resources you assign to the database are dedicated to that database and aren't shared with other databases in Azure.

notes.front: What are the two purchasing models for Azure SQL Database, and which one does Microsoft recommend?
notes.back: The vCore-based model, which is recommended, and the DTU-based model.
notes.explanation: The comparison page lists the vCore model first and labels it as the recommended one.
notes.source: Compare vCore and DTU-based purchasing models of Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Compare vCore and DTU-based purchasing models of Azure SQL Database”
notes.evidence: This article compares the two purchasing models for [Azure SQL Database](sql-database-paas-overview.md): - vCore-based purchasing model (recommended) - DTU-based purchasing model

notes.front: A team wants to choose compute and storage separately and use its existing SQL Server licences for a discount. Which purchasing model fits?
notes.back: The vCore-based purchasing model.
notes.explanation: vCore lets you pick compute and storage independently and supports Azure Hybrid Benefit; it is aimed at customers who value flexibility and control.
notes.source: Compare vCore and DTU-based purchasing models of Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Purchasing models”
notes.evidence: | vCore-based | This model allows you to independently choose compute and storage resources. The vCore-based purchasing model also allows you to use [Azure Hybrid Benefit](https://azure.microsoft.com/pricing/hybrid-benefit/) for SQL Server to save costs. | Customers who value flexibility, control, and transparency |

notes.front: vCore versus DTU: which purchasing model might suit a customer who wants preconfigured bundles and fixed monthly payments?
notes.back: The DTU-based model; vCore instead lets you choose resources individually.
notes.explanation: DTU packages compute with included storage in preset bundles, so the choice is a bundle size rather than separate resources.
notes.source: Compare vCore and DTU-based purchasing models of Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “DTU purchasing model”
notes.evidence: The DTU-based purchasing model offers a set of preconfigured bundles of compute resources and included storage to drive different levels of application performance. If you prefer the simplicity of a preconfigured bundle and fixed payments each month, the DTU-based model might be more suitable for your needs.

notes.front: A single database is moved from a 100-DTU compute size to a 200-DTU compute size. What happens to the resources available to it?
notes.back: They double.
notes.explanation: DTUs are most useful as a relative measure of resources across compute sizes and service tiers.
notes.source: DTU-based purchasing model overview (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Database transaction units (DTUs)”
notes.evidence: DTUs are most useful for understanding the relative resources that are allocated for databases at different compute sizes and service tiers. For example: - Doubling the DTUs by increasing the compute size of a database equates to doubling the set of resources available to that database.

notes.front: Which three service tiers does the DTU-based purchasing model offer?
notes.back: Basic, Standard and Premium.
notes.explanation: The DTU model is also available for elastic pools, in the same tiers.
notes.source: DTU-based purchasing model overview (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “DTU-based purchasing model overview”
notes.evidence: The DTU-based purchasing model is available in the Basic, Standard, and Premium service tiers. The DTU-based purchasing model is also available for elastic pools.

notes.front: How is the General Purpose service tier built?
notes.back: Compute is separated from storage; the database files live in Azure Blob storage.
notes.explanation: Blob storage transparently replicates the files, and the tier relies on that for availability and no data loss.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “General Purpose”
notes.evidence: The architectural model for the General Purpose service tier is based on a separation of compute and storage. This architectural model relies on the high availability and reliability of Azure Blob storage that transparently replicates database files and guarantees no data loss if underlying infrastructure failure happens.

notes.front: An internal booking app needs a fully managed database; storage latency of around 5 to 10 milliseconds is fine. Which vCore service tier fits?
notes.back: General Purpose.
notes.explanation: That latency range is exactly what the documentation gives for General Purpose, so there is no need to pay for Business Critical.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “When to choose the General Purpose service tier”
notes.evidence: If you need a fully managed database engine with a default SLA and storage latency between 5 ms and 10 ms, the General Purpose tier is the option for you.

notes.front: A trading system needs storage responses of 1 to 2 milliseconds on average and a free readable secondary for its reports. Which vCore service tier fits?
notes.back: Business Critical.
notes.explanation: Business Critical is designed for low-latency local storage, faster recovery and offloading reports to a free readable secondary replica.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “When to choose the Business Critical service tier”
notes.evidence: The Business Critical service tier is designed for applications that require low-latency responses from the underlying SSD storage (1-2 ms in average), faster recovery if the underlying infrastructure fails, or need to off-load reports, analytics, and read-only queries to the free of charge readable secondary replica of the primary database.

notes.front: About how much more does Business Critical cost than General Purpose, and what causes the difference?
notes.back: About 2.7 times as much, because three extra high-availability replicas are allocated automatically.
notes.explanation: The replicas provide high resiliency to failures and fast failovers; that is what the higher price buys.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Compute”
notes.evidence: Regardless of the compute tier, three additional high availability secondary replicas are automatically allocated in the Business Critical service tier to provide high resiliency to failures and fast failovers. These additional replicas make the cost approximately 2.7 times higher than it is in the General Purpose service tier.

notes.front: What sets the pricing of the Hyperscale service tier apart from the other Azure SQL Database tiers?
notes.back: It has no SQL software licence fee.
notes.explanation: For high-performance databases, the missing licence fee gives Hyperscale a significant price advantage.
notes.source: Hyperscale service tier (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Hyperscale service tier”
notes.evidence: Unlike other service tiers, Hyperscale has no SQL software license fee, which gives it a significant price advantage over other Azure SQL Database service tiers for high-performance databases.

notes.front: Hyperscale storage is allocated automatically between 10 gigabytes and {{c1::128 terabytes}}, growing as needed.
notes.explanation: You do not set a maximum data size; you pay for the storage actually allocated.
notes.source: Hyperscale service tier (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Hyperscale pricing model”
notes.evidence: You don't specify the max data size when configuring a Hyperscale database. In the Hyperscale tier, you pay for storage based on actual allocation. Storage is automatically allocated between 10 GB and 128 TB, and grows as needed.

notes.front: A single database is forecast to reach 60 terabytes within two years. Which Azure SQL Database service tier can hold it?
notes.back: Hyperscale.
notes.choices:
A) Hyperscale
B) Business Critical
C) General Purpose
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the overview's example range for a single database stops at 4 terabytes, and it names Hyperscale as the tier that scales up to 128 terabytes.
notes.explanation: Hyperscale lets a single database grow to 128 terabytes, well past the other tiers.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL Database? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Scalable performance and pools”
notes.evidence: For example, you can get 1 to 128 vCores, or 32 GB to 4 TB. The [Hyperscale service tier](service-tier-hyperscale.md) enables you to scale up to 128 TB, with fast backup and restore capabilities.

notes.front: In Hyperscale you choose from {{c1::0 to 4}} additional high-availability replicas.
notes.explanation: The number is a trade-off between the resilience the application needs and the cost.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Compute”
notes.evidence: In Hyperscale, customers control the number of additional high availability replicas from 0 to 4 to get the level of resiliency required by their applications while controlling costs.

notes.front: Provisioned versus serverless compute: how does each bill for compute?
notes.back: Provisioned: a fixed price per hour for the compute provisioned. Serverless: per second for the compute actually used.
notes.explanation: Serverless also scales its compute automatically with workload activity.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Compute”
notes.evidence: the **serverless compute tier** autoscales compute resources based on workload activity. - While the **provisioned compute tier** bills for the amount of compute provisioned at a fixed price per hour, the **serverless compute tier** bills for the amount of compute used, per second.

notes.front: In which service tiers is serverless compute available for Azure SQL Database?
notes.back: General Purpose and Hyperscale, in the vCore model only.
notes.explanation: Business Critical and the DTU tiers are left out, so a serverless database must sit in one of these two.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL Database? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Compute tiers”
notes.evidence: The serverless compute tier is available in the vCore purchasing model, in the General Purpose and Hyperscale service tiers.

notes.front: In which service tier are serverless auto-pause and auto-resume currently supported?
notes.back: Only General Purpose.
notes.explanation: A serverless Hyperscale database therefore scales compute automatically but does not pause.
notes.source: Serverless compute tier for Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Serverless compute tier for Azure SQL Database”
notes.evidence: Currently, auto-pause and auto-resume are only supported in the General Purpose service tier.

notes.front: What does a serverless database cost while it is paused?
notes.back: Only storage; the compute cost is zero.
notes.explanation: While running below the configured minimum, you still pay for the minimum vCores and memory.
notes.source: Serverless compute tier for Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Cost”
notes.evidence: - When compute usage is below the minimum limits you configure, the compute cost is based on the minimum vCores and minimum memory configured. - When the database is paused, the compute cost is zero and only storage costs are incurred.

notes.front: The serverless auto-pause delay defaults to {{c1::60 minutes}}, with a minimum of 15 minutes.
notes.explanation: The delay is how long the database must be inactive before pausing; it can reach seven days or be switched off.
notes.source: Serverless compute tier for Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Default settings”
notes.evidence:
|Auto-pause delay|Minimum: 15 minutes
Maximum: 10,080 minutes (seven days)
Increments: 1 minute
Disable auto-pause: -1|60 minutes|

notes.front: An order-processing database is busy and steady all day, and cannot tolerate delays while resuming from a pause. Which compute choice fits?
notes.back: Provisioned compute.
notes.choices:
A) Provisioned compute
B) Serverless compute in General Purpose
C) Serverless compute in Business Critical
notes.choicesExplained: B: serverless suits intermittent, unpredictable use that can accept a warm-up delay after idle periods. C: serverless is not offered in Business Critical.
notes.explanation: Regular, predictable use with high average utilisation, and no tolerance for resume delays, are both listed as reasons for provisioned compute.
notes.source: Serverless compute tier for Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Scenarios well suited for provisioned compute”
notes.evidence: - Single databases with more regular, predictable usage patterns and higher average compute utilization over time. - Databases that can't tolerate performance trade-offs resulting from more frequent memory trimming or delays in resuming from a paused state.

notes.front: How is an elastic pool billed?
notes.back: For each hour the pool exists, at its highest eDTU or vCore setting, with no per-database charge.
notes.explanation: Adding databases therefore adds no per-database fee; the pool’s size sets the bill whatever the usage.
notes.source: Elastic pools help you manage and scale multiple databases in Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “What are SQL elastic pools?”
notes.evidence: There's no per-database charge for elastic pools. You're billed for each hour a pool exists at the highest eDTU or vCores, regardless of usage or whether the pool was active for less than an hour.

notes.front: Which usage pattern makes databases good candidates for an elastic pool?
notes.back: Many databases with low average utilisation and infrequent spikes.
notes.explanation: Databases with persistent medium-high utilisation should not share a pool.
notes.source: Elastic pools help you manage and scale multiple databases in Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “When to consider a SQL Database elastic pool?”
notes.evidence: Pools are well suited for a large number of databases with specific utilization patterns. This pattern is characterized by low average utilization with infrequent utilization spikes for a given database. Conversely, multiple databases with persistent medium-high utilization shouldn't be placed in the same elastic pool.

notes.front: A software company gives each of its 400 customers a database. Most sit nearly idle but spike briefly at different times of day. What is the cost-effective design?
notes.back: Put the databases in an elastic pool.
notes.choices:
A) Put the databases in an elastic pool
B) Give each a single database sized for its peak
C) Give each a single database sized for its average
notes.choicesExplained: B: sizing every database for its peak overprovisions and overpays. C: sizing for the average saves money but hurts performance and customers during peaks.
notes.explanation: A pool gives each database the resources it needs when it needs them, from one shared budget.
notes.source: Elastic pools help you manage and scale multiple databases in Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “What are SQL elastic pools?”
notes.evidence: - Overprovision resources based on peak usage and overpay. - Underprovision to save cost at the expense of performance and customer satisfaction during peaks. Elastic pools solve this problem by ensuring that databases get the performance resources they need when they need them.

notes.front: One database in an elastic pool has consistently high utilisation that is affecting the other databases. What does Microsoft advise?
notes.back: Move it out of the pool and run it as a single database with a predictable amount of resources.
notes.explanation: Pools suit databases whose peaks are infrequent; a steadily busy one is better served with its own resources.
notes.source: DTU-based purchasing model overview (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Elastic database transaction units (eDTUs)”
notes.evidence: If a database has consistently high resource utilization that affects other databases in the pool, move it out of the pool and configure it as a single database with a predictable amount of required resources.

notes.front: Horizontal versus vertical scaling of Azure SQL databases: what does each change?
notes.back: Horizontal (scaling out) adds or removes databases; vertical (scaling up) changes one database’s compute size.
notes.explanation: Sharding is a common way to scale out, partitioning data across identically structured databases.
notes.source: Scale out with Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Horizontal and vertical scaling”
notes.evidence: Horizontal scaling refers to adding or removing databases in order to adjust capacity or overall performance, also called "scaling out." Sharding, in which data is partitioned across a collection of identically structured databases, is a common way to implement horizontal scaling.

notes.front: Month-end reports overload a database, so the team raises it from 4 to 8 vCores. Which kind of scaling is that?
notes.back: Vertical scaling (scaling up).
notes.explanation: Only one database’s compute size changes; no databases are added.
notes.source: Scale out with Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Horizontal and vertical scaling”
notes.evidence: Vertical scaling refers to increasing or decreasing the compute size of an individual database, also known as "scaling up."

notes.front: What are two reasons the documentation gives for sharding?
notes.back: Any two of, among others: data too large for one database; throughput beyond one database; tenants needing physical isolation.
notes.explanation: Each is a limit of a single database that spreading the data over many databases removes.
notes.source: Scale out with Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Sharding”
notes.evidence: - The total amount of data is too large to fit within the constraints of an individual database - The transaction throughput of the overall workload exceeds the capabilities of an individual database - Tenants might require physical isolation from each other, so separate databases are needed for each tenant

notes.front: A retailer’s order data must be held in the country where each order was placed, for compliance. Which approach fits?
notes.back: Shard the data across identically structured databases in each geography.
notes.choices:
A) Shard the data across identically structured databases in each geography
B) Scale the single database up to a larger compute size
C) Turn on read scale-out
notes.choicesExplained: B: a bigger single database still holds all the data in one place. C: read replicas are copies of the same database, not a way to place data in different geographies.
notes.explanation: Keeping sections of the data in different geographies for compliance is one of the listed reasons for sharding.
notes.source: Scale out with Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Sharding”
notes.evidence: - Different sections of a database might need to reside in different geographies for compliance, performance, or geopolitical reasons.

notes.front: With read scale-out enabled, how does an application send its connection to a read-only replica?
notes.back: By setting `ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly` in its connection string.
notes.explanation: Leaving the option out, or using the default `ReadWrite`, sends the connection to the read-write replica.
notes.source: Use read-only replicas to offload read-only query workloads (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Connect to a read-only replica”
notes.evidence: Specifically, if the `ApplicationIntent` value is `ReadWrite` (the default value), the connection is directed to the read-write replica. This is identical to the behavior when `ApplicationIntent` isn't included in the connection string. If the `ApplicationIntent` value is `ReadOnly`, the connection is routed to a read-only replica.

notes.front: A General Purpose database needs a readable replica for reporting. Can it use read scale-out?
notes.back: No. General Purpose has no replicas in its high-availability design, so read scale-out is unavailable.
notes.explanation: Geo-replicas can provide similar functionality in these tiers.
notes.source: Use read-only replicas to offload read-only query workloads (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Use read-only replicas to offload read-only query workloads”
notes.evidence: The High Availability architecture of Basic, Standard, and General Purpose service tiers doesn't include any replicas. The *read scale-out* feature isn't available in these service tiers. However, when using Azure SQL Database, [geo-replicas](active-geo-replication-overview.md) can provide similar functionality in these service tiers.

notes.front: In which Azure SQL Database service tiers is read scale-out enabled by default?
notes.back: Premium, Business Critical and Hyperscale.
notes.explanation: It cannot be enabled in Basic, Standard or General Purpose.
notes.source: Use read-only replicas to offload read-only query workloads (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Enable and disable read scale-out for SQL Database”
notes.evidence: For SQL Database, read scale-out is enabled by default on Premium, Business Critical, and Hyperscale service tiers. Read scale-out can't be enabled in Basic, Standard, or General Purpose service tiers.

notes.front: A checkout page saves an order and immediately reads it back to show a confirmation. Should that read go to a read-only replica?
notes.back: No; send it to the primary, because a replica may not yet show the new order.
notes.explanation: Reads from replicas lag the primary by a variable amount, so data just written may not be visible there yet.
notes.source: Use read-only replicas to offload read-only query workloads (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Data consistency”
notes.evidence: Likewise, if an application changes data using a read-write session on the primary and immediately reads it using a read-only session on a read-only replica, it is possible that the latest changes aren't immediately visible.

notes.front: Is a newly created Azure SQL database encrypted with TDE?
notes.back: Yes, by default, using service-managed transparent data encryption.
notes.explanation: Databases created from an encrypted source by restore, geo-replication or copy are encrypted by default too.
notes.source: Transparent data encryption for SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Transparent data encryption for SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics”
notes.evidence: All newly created SQL databases are encrypted by default by using service-managed transparent data encryption. When the database source is encrypted, the target databases created through **restore**, **geo-replication**, and **database copy** are encrypted by default.

notes.front: In customer-managed TDE, where is the TDE protector kept?
notes.back: In a customer-owned Azure Key Vault, which it never leaves.
notes.explanation: This arrangement is also called bring your own key.
notes.source: Transparent data encryption for SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Customer-managed transparent data encryption - Bring Your Own Key”
notes.evidence: Customer-managed TDE is also referred to as Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) support for TDE. In this scenario, the TDE Protector that encrypts the DEK is a customer-managed asymmetric key, which is stored in a customer-owned and managed Azure Key Vault (Azure's cloud-based external key management system) and never leaves the key vault.

notes.front: A security team removes the SQL server’s permissions on the key vault that holds its customer-managed TDE protector. What happens to the database?
notes.back: It becomes inaccessible.
notes.explanation: With customer-managed keys, the server needs permission on the vault to decrypt the database encryption key.
notes.source: Transparent data encryption for SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Customer-managed transparent data encryption - Bring Your Own Key”
notes.evidence: SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse need to be granted permissions to the customer-owned key vault to decrypt and encrypt the DEK. If permissions of the server to the key vault are revoked, a database will be inaccessible, and all data is encrypted.

notes.front: An auditor requires a company to control rotation of the keys that protect its SQL database encryption, with key management separated from data management. Which option fits?
notes.back: Customer-managed TDE with keys in Azure Key Vault.
notes.choices:
A) Customer-managed TDE with keys in Azure Key Vault
B) Service-managed TDE
C) Dynamic data masking
notes.choicesExplained: B: with service-managed TDE, Microsoft rotates the certificates itself. C: masking hides values in query results; it does not encrypt stored data.
notes.explanation: Key Vault integration puts key rotation in the customer’s hands and supports separation of duties between keys and data.
notes.source: Transparent data encryption for SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Customer-managed transparent data encryption - Bring Your Own Key”
notes.evidence: users can control key management tasks including key rotations, key vault permissions, key backups, and enable auditing/reporting on all TDE protectors using Azure Key Vault or Azure Managed HSM functionality. Azure Key Vault and Azure Managed HSM provide central key management, leverages tightly monitored HSMs, and enables separation of duties between management of keys and data

notes.front: Who sees unmasked data despite a dynamic data masking policy?
notes.back: Users listed as excluded from masking, and administrators such as server admin, Microsoft Entra admin and db_owner.
notes.explanation: The exclusion list can include identities from Microsoft Entra, not only SQL logins.
notes.source: Dynamic data masking (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Dynamic data masking policy”
notes.evidence: A set of SQL users, which can include identities from Microsoft Entra ID, that get unmasked data in the SQL query results. Users with administrative rights like server admin, Microsoft Entra admin, and db_owner role can view the original data without any mask.

notes.front: Team leads run a report that must hide employees’ salaries in its results, while the payroll service reading the same table still needs the real figures. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Dynamic data masking, with the payroll service’s user excluded from masking.
notes.choices:
A) Dynamic data masking, excluding the payroll service’s user
B) Transparent data encryption
C) Read scale-out for the team leads
notes.choicesExplained: B: TDE protects files at rest; anyone allowed to query still sees real values. C: a read replica holds the same unmasked data.
notes.explanation: Masking hides values in query results for most users while excluded users get the real data, and the stored table is unchanged.
notes.source: Dynamic data masking (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Dynamic data masking policy”
notes.evidence: **SQL users excluded from masking:** A set of SQL users, which can include identities from Microsoft Entra ID, that get unmasked data in the SQL query results.

notes.front: Transparent data encryption versus dynamic data masking: what does each guard against?
notes.back: TDE: offline access to data at rest. Masking: exposure of sensitive values to nonprivileged users in query results.
notes.explanation: Masking changes what a query returns, not what is stored; encryption at rest is a separate protection.
notes.source: Dynamic data masking (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Dynamic data masking”
notes.evidence: Dynamic data masking limits sensitive data exposure by masking it to nonprivileged users.

notes.front: How long can an Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server stay stopped?
notes.back: Up to seven days, unless you start it again sooner.
notes.explanation: Compute billing ends as soon as the server stops, which helps for development, testing and predictable time-bound workloads.
notes.source: What is Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server? (Microsoft Learn), “Stop and start server to lower TCO”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server

notes.front: Which Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server compute tier suits low-cost development with few concurrent users?
notes.back: Burstable.
notes.explanation: General Purpose and Memory Optimized are meant for production work needing high concurrency, scale and predictable performance.
notes.source: What is Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server? (Microsoft Learn), “Adjust performance and scale within seconds”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server

notes.front: Azure SQL Managed Instance versus SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines: who configures, patches and upgrades the database software?
notes.back: Azure does it for Managed Instance; on a virtual machine you decide when and do it yourself.
notes.explanation: Automatic patching is one way the platform options reduce administration costs.
notes.source: What is Azure SQL? (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Billing and licensing basics”
notes.evidence: With **SQL Database** and **SQL Managed Instance**, the database software is automatically configured, patched, and upgraded by Azure, which reduces your administration costs.
uses: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

notes.front: General Purpose versus Business Critical: where do the database files sit?
notes.back: General Purpose: in Azure Blob storage, apart from compute. Business Critical: on locally attached solid-state storage on the same node.
notes.explanation: Keeping the engine and its files on one node is what gives Business Critical its low latency.
notes.source: vCore purchasing model - Azure SQL Database (MicrosoftDocs sql-docs), “Business Critical”
notes.evidence: Both the database engine process and underlying .mdf/.ldf files are placed on the same node with locally attached SSD storage, providing low latency to your workload.
